claim: CLUH is a post-transcriptional regulator of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation and several metabolic pathways.
source: CLUH (clustered mitochondria homolog) is a post-transcriptional regulator of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation and several metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to previous work (Gao et al., 2014; Schatton et al., 2017).

claim: CLUH binds the SPAG5 mRNA.
source: We show a role of CLUH in regulating the expression of astrin, which is involved in metaphase to anaphase progression, centrosome integrity, and mTORC1 inhibition. We find that CLUH binds both the SPAG5 mRNA and its product astrin, and controls the synthesis and the stability of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding directly in the abstract and provides experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: CLUH binds the astrin protein.
source: We find that CLUH binds both the SPAG5 mRNA and its product astrin, and controls the synthesis and the stability of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CLUH controls the synthesis of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
source: We find that CLUH binds both the SPAG5 mRNA and its product astrin, and controls the synthesis and the stability of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolic labeling experiments in Figure 2H-I.

claim: CLUH controls the stability of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
source: We find that CLUH binds both the SPAG5 mRNA and its product astrin, and controls the synthesis and the stability of the full-length astrin-1 isoform.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cycloheximide chase experiments in Figure 2A-D.

claim: CLUH interacts with astrin-1 specifically during interphase.
source: We show that CLUH interacts with astrin-1 specifically during interphase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoprecipitation experiments in synchronized cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Astrin-depleted cells show mTORC1 hyperactivation.
source: Astrin-depleted cells show mTORC1 hyperactivation and enhanced anabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Astrin-depleted cells show enhanced anabolism.
source: Astrin-depleted cells show mTORC1 hyperactivation and enhanced anabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5D-H.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH show decreased astrin levels.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking CLUH show decreased astrin levels and increased mTORC1 signaling, but cannot sustain anaplerotic and anabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH show increased mTORC1 signaling.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking CLUH show decreased astrin levels and increased mTORC1 signaling, but cannot sustain anaplerotic and anabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH cannot sustain anaplerotic pathways.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking CLUH show decreased astrin levels and increased mTORC1 signaling, but cannot sustain anaplerotic and anabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6C showing decreased TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH cannot sustain anabolic pathways.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking CLUH show decreased astrin levels and increased mTORC1 signaling, but cannot sustain anaplerotic and anabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6E, F showing decreased nucleotides and polyamines.

claim: In absence of CLUH, cells fail to grow during G1.
source: In absence of CLUH, cells fail to grow during G1, and progress faster through the cell cycle, indicating dysregulated matching of growth, metabolism, and cell cycling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell size measurements in Figure 7J.

claim: In absence of CLUH, cells progress faster through the cell cycle.
source: In absence of CLUH, cells fail to grow during G1, and progress faster through the cell cycle, indicating dysregulated matching of growth, metabolism, and cell cycling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7D-G.

claim: CLUH plays a role in coupling growth signaling pathways and mitochondrial metabolism with cell cycle progression.
source: Our data reveal a role of CLUH in coupling growth signaling pathways and mitochondrial metabolism with cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Astrin was detected as an RNA-independent interactor of endogenous CLUH in a pull-down experiment in HeLa cells after SILAC followed by mass spectrometry.
source: Surprisingly, we also detected astrin as an RNA-independent interactor of endogenous CLUH in a pull-down experiment in HeLa cells after stable isotope labeling in cell culture (SILAC) followed by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The interaction between CLUH and astrin was confirmed by reciprocal immunoprecipitations using antibodies against human CLUH and astrin, followed by western blot.
source: Reciprocal immunoprecipitations (IPs) using antibodies against human CLUH and astrin, followed by western blot, confirmed the interaction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: CLUH binds kinastrin.
source: Binding was also validated between CLUH and kinastrin (also known as SKAP), a known astrin interactor (Figure 1B; Schmidt et al., 2010; Dunsch et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1B.

claim: Astrin appears as two isoforms (astrin-1 and astrin-2) in western blots.
source: Astrin appears as two isoforms (hereafter referred to as astrin-1 and astrin-2) in western blots, and CLUH interacts preferentially with the slower migrating isoform, astrin-1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: CLUH interacts preferentially with astrin-1.
source: Astrin appears as two isoforms (hereafter referred to as astrin-1 and astrin-2) in western blots, and CLUH interacts preferentially with the slower migrating isoform, astrin-1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1A.

claim: The SPAG5 mRNA contains five in-frame ATGs downstream of the first ATG.
source: On closer inspection of the SPAG5 mRNA, we noticed the presence of five in-frame ATGs downstream of the first ATG (hereafter referred to as ATG2-6), which could serve as alternative translation start codons (with moderate and good Kozak sequences) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An upstream ORF within the SPAG5 5′ UTR could influence translation from the downstream ATGs.
source: Moreover, an upstream ORF within the SPAG5 5′ UTR (Figure 1C) could influence translation from the downstream ATGs as reported for other genes (Morris and Geballe, 2000; Young and Wek, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous work on uORFs.

claim: When the uATG of SPAG5 was mutagenized to GGG, the expression of astrin-2 was suppressed.
source: When we expressed the uATGGGG-SPAG5 construct, the expression of astrin-2 was suppressed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 1D.

claim: Mutagenesis of ATG1 confirmed the existence of a downstream alternative translation start site.
source: Furthermore, mutagenesis of ATG1 confirmed the existence of a downstream alternative translation start site (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 1D.

claim: Astrin-2 is the product of alternative translation starting from ATG3-5.
source: Overexpression of the constructs harboring mutagenized downstream ATGs revealed that astrin-2 is the product of alternative translation starting from ATG3-5 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 1E.

claim: CLUH binds within the N-terminus of astrin-1.
source: An interaction was observed only with full-length astrin, proving that CLUH binds within the N-terminus of astrin-1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1F.

claim: Kinastrin has no binding preference to any of the two astrin isoforms.
source: In contrast, the astrin interactor kinastrin has no binding preference to any of the two astrin isoforms, consistent with the previously mapped interaction domain between these two proteins (residues 482–693 of astrin) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Dunsch et al., 2011; Friese et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CLUH still interacts with astrin-1 upon kinastrin depletion.
source: CLUH still interacts with astrin-1 upon kinastrin depletion, suggesting that kinastrin is not required for the interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Endogenous CLUH was recruited to astrin-1 but not astrin-2-positive structures.
source: Endogenous CLUH was characteristically recruited to astrin-1 but not astrin-2-positive structures, in agreement with the biochemical characterization of this interaction (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunofluorescence images in Figure 1G.

claim: In polysome profiles performed after chemical crosslinking, CLUH migrated in lighter fractions, as well as in fractions containing the monosome and polysomes.
source: In polysome profiles performed after chemical crosslinking, CLUH migrated in lighter fractions, as well as in fractions containing the monosome and polysomes, while astrin and kinastrin were only detected in the lighter fractions (Figure 1H), indicating the existence of distinct CLUH complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in polysome profiling data in Figure 1H.

claim: Astrin and kinastrin were only detected in the lighter fractions of polysome profiles.
source: In polysome profiles performed after chemical crosslinking, CLUH migrated in lighter fractions, as well as in fractions containing the monosome and polysomes, while astrin and kinastrin were only detected in the lighter fractions (Figure 1H), indicating the existence of distinct CLUH complexes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in polysome profiling data in Figure 1H.

claim: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin is decreased in abundance.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are decreased in abundance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: In absence of CLUH, astrin-1 is decreased in abundance.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are decreased in abundance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: In absence of CLUH, astrin-2 abundance is not decreased.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are decreased in abundance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin is highly unstable.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are highly unstable (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in cycloheximide chase data in Figure 2A-D.

claim: In absence of CLUH, astrin-1 is highly unstable.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are highly unstable (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in cycloheximide chase data in Figure 2A-D.

claim: In absence of CLUH, astrin-2 is not highly unstable.
source: In absence of CLUH, kinastrin and astrin-1, but not astrin-2, are highly unstable (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in cycloheximide chase data in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG132 treatment in CLUH KO HeLa cells fully rescued kinastrin levels.
source: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG132 treatment in CLUH KO HeLa cells fully rescued kinastrin and partially astrin-1 levels (Figure 2A, E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 2A, E-G.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG132 treatment in CLUH KO HeLa cells partially rescued astrin-1 levels.
source: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG132 treatment in CLUH KO HeLa cells fully rescued kinastrin and partially astrin-1 levels (Figure 2A, E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 2A, E-G.

claim: Newly synthesized astrin-1 is reduced in absence of CLUH.
source: We observed that newly synthesized astrin-1 is reduced in absence of CLUH to a greater extent than astrin-2, possibly also reflecting the decreased stability of this isoform (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolic labeling data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: SPAG5 mRNA was less stable in absence of CLUH.
source: SPAG5 mRNA was less stable in absence of CLUH, whereas steady-state levels and EU incorporation were unaffected (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in mRNA decay data in Figure 2J-L.

claim: SPAG5 mRNA steady-state levels were unaffected in absence of CLUH.
source: SPAG5 mRNA was less stable in absence of CLUH, whereas steady-state levels and EU incorporation were unaffected (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in qRT-PCR data in Figure 2J.

claim: SPAG5 mRNA EU incorporation was unaffected in absence of CLUH.
source: SPAG5 mRNA was less stable in absence of CLUH, whereas steady-state levels and EU incorporation were unaffected (Figure 2J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in EU incorporation data in Figure 2K.

claim: Astrin-1 was more abundant in S and G2 phases.
source: Astrin-1, but not astrin-2, was more abundant in S and G2, while CLUH levels were similar in the different phases of the cell cycle (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: CLUH levels were similar in the different phases of the cell cycle.
source: Astrin-1, but not astrin-2, was more abundant in S and G2, while CLUH levels were similar in the different phases of the cell cycle (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: Both astrin isoforms are phosphorylated at multiple sites, leading to slower migration in SDS–PAGE in prometaphase.
source: Both astrin isoforms are phosphorylated at multiple sites, leading to slower migration in sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE) in prometaphase (PM) (Figure 3A; Chang et al., 2001; Cheng et al., 2008; Chiu et al., 2014; Chung et al., 2016; Geraghty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous work and shown in western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: The CLUH/astrin-1 complex is enriched in S and G2 phases but not detected in prometaphase.
source: The CLUH/astrin-1 complex is enriched in S and G2 phases but not detected in PM, indicating that CLUH preferentially interacts with unmodified astrin-1 in interphase and that the interaction might be controlled by the phosphorylation status of astrin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3A.

claim: CLUH preferentially interacts with unmodified astrin-1 in interphase.
source: The CLUH/astrin-1 complex is enriched in S and G2 phases but not detected in PM, indicating that CLUH preferentially interacts with unmodified astrin-1 in interphase and that the interaction might be controlled by the phosphorylation status of astrin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3A.

claim: The interaction between CLUH and astrin-1 might be controlled by the phosphorylation status of astrin.
source: The CLUH/astrin-1 complex is enriched in S and G2 phases but not detected in PM, indicating that CLUH preferentially interacts with unmodified astrin-1 in interphase and that the interaction might be controlled by the phosphorylation status of astrin (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Results section based on the observation that the interaction is lost when astrin is phosphorylated.

claim: Astrin-1 and kinastrin were confirmed as highly enriched interactors of CLUH in G2-synchronized cells by mass spectrometry.
source: This experiment confirmed astrin-1 and kinastrin as highly enriched interactors of CLUH (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in mass spectrometry data in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Proteins previously shown to be part of the astrin/kinastrin complex were detected in the CLUH immunoprecipitate.
source: In addition, proteins previously shown to be part of the astrin/kinastrin complex, such as MYCBP, or linking the complex to the microtubule cytoskeleton were also detected in the precipitate. Among these proteins are CLASP1 and 2, two microtubule plus-end binding proteins, and DYNLL1, a retrograde motor protein (Manning et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2010; Dunsch et al., 2011; Kern et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2017; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous work and shown in mass spectrometry data in Figure 3B.

claim: Among top CLUH interactors, the centrosomal proteins CEP170B and CEP44 were found.
source: Interestingly, among top CLUH interactors, we found the centrosomal proteins CEP170B and CEP44, suggesting a link of CLUH with the centrosome and the microtubules (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in mass spectrometry data in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Overexpressed astrin-1 can accumulate at the centrosome.
source: This suggests that overexpressed astrin-1 can accumulate at the centrosome, but also at non centrosomal structures.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: Endogenous CLUH is not a constitutive component of the centrosome.
source: CLUH and CEP43 stainings did not overlap in unsynchronized cells (Figure 3E), indicating that CLUH is not a constitutive component of the centrosome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: Mitochondrial distribution was indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Mitochondrial distribution, morphology, ultrastructure, and mtDNA levels were indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Mitochondrial morphology was indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Mitochondrial distribution, morphology, ultrastructure, and mtDNA levels were indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Mitochondrial ultrastructure was indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Mitochondrial distribution, morphology, ultrastructure, and mtDNA levels were indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in electron microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mtDNA levels were indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Mitochondrial distribution, morphology, ultrastructure, and mtDNA levels were indistinguishable in WT, SPAG5, and KNSTRN ind-KO cells (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: Respiratory supercomplexes containing complexes I and III assembled normally in SPAG5 and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Furthermore, respiratory supercomplexes containing complexes I and III assembled normally in these cells, and in-gel activity of complex I was similar to control cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in BN-PAGE data in Figure 4D.

claim: In-gel activity of complex I was similar to control cells in SPAG5 and KNSTRN ind-KO cells.
source: Furthermore, respiratory supercomplexes containing complexes I and III assembled normally in these cells, and in-gel activity of complex I was similar to control cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in BN-PAGE data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH displayed a reduction of assembled supercomplexes I–III.
source: In contrast, cells lacking CLUH displayed a reduction of assembled supercomplexes I–III, decreased activity of complex I, and abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in BN-PAGE data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH displayed decreased activity of complex I.
source: In contrast, cells lacking CLUH displayed a reduction of assembled supercomplexes I–III, decreased activity of complex I, and abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in BN-PAGE data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH displayed abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure.
source: In contrast, cells lacking CLUH displayed a reduction of assembled supercomplexes I–III, decreased activity of complex I, and abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in electron microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CLUH controls mitochondrial function independent from the interaction with astrin-1 or kinastrin.
source: These data indicate that CLUH controls mitochondrial function independent from the interaction with astrin-1 or kinastrin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on the observation that astrin/kinastrin depletion does not recapitulate CLUH KO mitochondrial phenotypes.

claim: Astrin depletion caused a slight decrease of proteins encoded by CLUH mRNA targets.
source: Notably, CLUH levels were unaffected by the loss of its interactors (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3). Astrin depletion caused a slight decrease of proteins encoded by CLUH mRNA targets (Figure 5A; marked in blue).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in proteomics data in Figure 5A.

claim: Downregulated KEGG pathways in SPAG5 ind-KO cells largely overlapped with metabolic pathways affected by CLUH deletion.
source: Downregulated KEGG pathways, analyzed using the EnrichR webtool (using a generous cutoff of p ≤ 0.05; q ≤ 0.15) (Chen et al., 2013; Kuleshov et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2021), largely overlapped with metabolic pathways affected by CLUH deletion (TCA cycle, fatty acid, and amino acid degradation; Figure 5B; Schatton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in pathway analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Metabolic pathways connected to nucleotide biosynthesis were upregulated in SPAG5 ind-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, metabolic pathways connected to nucleotide biosynthesis (purine and pyrimidine metabolism), the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and glycolysis were upregulated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in pathway analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: The pentose phosphate pathway was upregulated in SPAG5 ind-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, metabolic pathways connected to nucleotide biosynthesis (purine and pyrimidine metabolism), the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and glycolysis were upregulated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in pathway analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Glycolysis was upregulated in SPAG5 ind-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, metabolic pathways connected to nucleotide biosynthesis (purine and pyrimidine metabolism), the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and glycolysis were upregulated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in pathway analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: mTORC1 appeared as one of the most enriched terms in pathway analysis of perturbed proteins in SPAG5 ind-KO cells.
source: Furthermore, mTORC1 appeared as one of the most enriched terms in pathway analysis of perturbed proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in pathway analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: mTORC1 is hyperactive in SPAG5 ind-KOs upon starvation for 8 hr in HBSS.
source: We confirmed that mTORC1 is hyperactive in SPAG5 ind-KOs upon starvation for 8 hr in HBSS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to accumulation of several glycolytic intermediates.
source: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to more prominent alterations of the metabolome, with accumulation of several glycolytic intermediates, lactate, and sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, in agreement with high glycolytic rate and an increase in the PPP (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to accumulation of lactate.
source: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to more prominent alterations of the metabolome, with accumulation of several glycolytic intermediates, lactate, and sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, in agreement with high glycolytic rate and an increase in the PPP (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to accumulation of sedoheptulose-7-phosphate.
source: Upon starvation, SPAG5 depletion led to more prominent alterations of the metabolome, with accumulation of several glycolytic intermediates, lactate, and sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, in agreement with high glycolytic rate and an increase in the PPP (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5E.

claim: The TCA cycle intermediates citrate, isocitrate, and malate were increased in SPAG5 ind-KO cells upon starvation.
source: In addition, the TCA cycle intermediates citrate, isocitrate, and malate were increased (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5F.

claim: Several nucleotides accumulated in astrin-deficient cells upon starvation.
source: Both the TCA cycle and the PPP intermediates are crucial for synthesis of nucleotides, several of which accumulated in astrin-deficient cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5G.

claim: Ornithine was increased in SPAG5 ind-KO cells upon starvation.
source: Amino acid levels were unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F), with the exception of an increase of ornithine, a precursor of polyamines, which were also more abundant (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5H.

claim: Polyamines were more abundant in SPAG5 ind-KO cells upon starvation.
source: Amino acid levels were unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F), with the exception of an increase of ornithine, a precursor of polyamines, which were also more abundant (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5H.

claim: KNSTRN ind-KO cells did not show detectable metabolic differences to control cells upon starvation.
source: KNSTRN ind-KO cells did not show detectable metabolic differences to control cells (Figure 5D–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 5D-H.

claim: Cells depleted of astrin engage in anabolic pathways linked to cell growth despite starvation.
source: Together, our data show that cells depleted of astrin, despite starvation, engage in anabolic pathways linked to cell growth, in agreement with hyperactivated mTORC1 signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: Targeted metabolomics revealed a prominent decrease of the PPP intermediate sedoheptulose-7-phosphate in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: Targeted metabolomics revealed a prominent decrease of the PPP intermediate sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, and a significant increase of pyruvate (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6B.

claim: Pyruvate was significantly increased in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: Targeted metabolomics revealed a prominent decrease of the PPP intermediate sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, and a significant increase of pyruvate (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6C.

claim: The intermediates of the first part of the TCA cycle (citrate, aconitate, and isocitrate) were decreased in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: The intermediates of the first part of the TCA cycle (citrate, aconitate, and isocitrate) were decreased (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6C.

claim: Most amino acids that feed into the TCA cycle were decreased in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: In addition, most amino acids that feed into the TCA cycle were decreased (Figure 6D), including aspartate, which is mainly produced by oxaloacetate and is an important precursor of pyrimidines (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6D.

claim: Glutamine was elevated in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: Glutamine was instead elevated, as well as α-ketoglutarate (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6C, D.

claim: α-ketoglutarate was elevated in CLUH KO cells upon starvation.
source: Glutamine was instead elevated, as well as α-ketoglutarate (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6C.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH showed a perturbation of polyamines metabolism, with a prominent reduction of spermidine.
source: In addition, cells lacking CLUH showed a perturbation of polyamines metabolism, with a prominent reduction of spermidine, and decreased levels of some nucleotides, especially inosine monophosphate (IMP), the first nucleotide in the synthesis pathway of purines (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6E.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH showed decreased levels of some nucleotides, especially inosine monophosphate (IMP).
source: In addition, cells lacking CLUH showed a perturbation of polyamines metabolism, with a prominent reduction of spermidine, and decreased levels of some nucleotides, especially inosine monophosphate (IMP), the first nucleotide in the synthesis pathway of purines (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in metabolomics data in Figure 6F.

claim: Upon starvation CLUH KO cells fail to maintain the TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerosis).
source: Thus, upon starvation CLUH KO cells fail to maintain the TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerosis), and surprisingly show defects also in other anabolic pathways that are linked to cell growth and are regulated by mTORC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: CLUH KO cells show defects in anabolic pathways that are linked to cell growth and are regulated by mTORC1.
source: Thus, upon starvation CLUH KO cells fail to maintain the TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerosis), and surprisingly show defects also in other anabolic pathways that are linked to cell growth and are regulated by mTORC1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: The metabolic profile of CLUH KO cells is strikingly opposite to that of SPAG5 ind-KO cells.
source: This metabolic profile is strikingly opposite to that of SPAG5 ind-KO cells, and indicate that the mTORC1 hyperactivation in absence of CLUH is not reflected in the cellular metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on comparison of metabolomics data.

claim: The mTORC1 hyperactivation in absence of CLUH is not reflected in the cellular metabolic rewiring.
source: This metabolic profile is strikingly opposite to that of SPAG5 ind-KO cells, and indicate that the mTORC1 hyperactivation in absence of CLUH is not reflected in the cellular metabolic rewiring.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: CLUH plays an important role in the mTORC1-dependent rewiring of cellular metabolism.
source: This data points to an important role of CLUH in the mTORC1-dependent rewiring of cellular metabolism, by supporting mitochondrial anaplerotic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on metabolomics data.

claim: CLUH KO cells showed a reduction of the levels of phosphorylated retinoblastoma (pRB1-Ser807/811).
source: Assessment of unsynchronized cells using markers for different phases of the cell cycle showed a reduction of the levels of phosphorylated retinoblastoma (pRB1-Ser807/811) in absence of CLUH (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 7A, B.

claim: CLUH KO cells showed different dynamics in cell cycle progression compared to wildtype cells.
source: CLUH KO cells showed different dynamics in cell cycle progression compared to wildtype cells (significant changes in genotype × time in G0/G1, S, and G2/M phases; Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 7D-G.

claim: CLUH KO cells cycled faster than control cells.
source: Surprisingly, CLUH KO cells cycled faster than control cells, with more cells already in G2/M 3 hr after the release and more cells entering the next cell cycle at 8 hr after release (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in flow cytometry data in Figure 7D-G.

claim: In absence of CLUH, pRB1-Ser807/811 increased less during the progression of the cell cycle and peaked earlier compared to wildtype cells.
source: In absence of CLUH, pRB1-Ser807/811 increased less during the progression of the cell cycle and peaked earlier compared to wildtype cells (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 7H, I.

claim: Cyclin D3 showed a flattener profile in the CLUH KO compared to wildtype cells during the first 8 hr after release.
source: Cyclin D3 also showed a flattener profile in the KO compared to wildtype cells during the first 8 hr after release (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 7H, I.

claim: CLUH KO cells have the ability to overcome cell cycle checkpoints at the G1/S transition.
source: These results hint at the ability of CLUH KO cells to overcome cell cycle checkpoints at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Results section based on cell cycle progression data.

claim: Astrin-1 levels dropped prematurely in CLUH KO cells 6 hr after synchronization.
source: Remarkably, while CLUH levels did not change during the cell cycle, astrin-1 and to a lesser extent astrin-2 levels dropped prematurely in CLUH KO cells 6 hr after synchronization, a time point where most cells are in G2 (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in western blot data in Figure 7H, I.

claim: CLUH KO cells showed a reduced cell size at all time points during the release from synchronization.
source: CLUH KO cells showed a reduced cell size at all time points during the release, in agreement with the defective growth pathways detected by the metabolomics (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in cell size measurements in Figure 7J.

claim: Upon loss of CLUH, HeLa cells escape the growth and energy checkpoint at the end of G1 and proceed faster through the cell cycle.
source: Thus, upon loss of CLUH, HeLa cells escape the growth and energy checkpoint at the end of G1 and proceed faster through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on cell cycle progression and cell size data.

claim: CLUH is a novel coordinator of mitochondrial activity with the cell cycle progression.
source: Our results thus identify CLUH as a novel coordinator of mitochondrial activity with the cell cycle progression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Results section based on all the data presented.

claim: The two astrin isoforms arise by alternative translation initiation.
source: We demonstrate that the two astrin isoforms arise by alternative translation initiation, and are regulated by the presence of an uORF and downstream AUGs with good Kozak sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 1D, E.

claim: The two astrin isoforms are regulated by the presence of an uORF and downstream AUGs with good Kozak sequences.
source: We demonstrate that the two astrin isoforms arise by alternative translation initiation, and are regulated by the presence of an uORF and downstream AUGs with good Kozak sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 1D, E.

claim: CLUH interacts only with the full-length astrin-1 protein.
source: Intriguingly, CLUH interacts only with the full-length astrin-1 protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1A, F.

claim: The N-terminal region of astrin is an unstructured domain that is dispensable for interaction with kinastrin, DYNLL1, MYCBP, and the kinetochore.
source: The N-terminal region of astrin is an unstructured domain that is dispensable for interaction with kinastrin, DYNLL1, MYCBP, and the kinetochore (Kern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: PLK1 kinase interacts with and phosphorylates the astrin N-terminus, an important step to stabilize the kinetochore–microtubule attachment.
source: Recently, the PLK1 kinase has been shown to interact with and phosphorylate the astrin N-terminus, an important step to stabilize the kinetochore–microtubule attachment (Geraghty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to recent work.

claim: N-terminal phosphorylations are responsible for the lack of interaction of CLUH and astrin-1 in prometaphase.
source: Based on our findings, we speculate that N-terminal phosphorylations are responsible for the lack of interaction of CLUH and astrin-1 in PM.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section based on the observation that the interaction is lost when astrin is phosphorylated.

claim: Astrin detaches from CLUH during mitosis when it is required for metaphase to anaphase progression.
source: Thus, astrin detaches from CLUH during mitosis when it is required for metaphase to anaphase progression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on the cell cycle-dependent interaction data.

claim: CLUH appears to regulate astrin-1 expression at multiple levels.
source: Interestingly, CLUH appears to regulate astrin-1 expression at multiple levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data on mRNA stability, protein synthesis, and protein stability.

claim: During cytokinesis the E3-ubiquitin ligase MID2 ubiquitinates astrin, targeting it for proteosomal degradation.
source: It is known that during cytokinesis the E3-ubiquitin ligase MID2 ubiquitinates astrin, targeting it for proteosomal degradation (Gholkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: CLUH may be implicated in supporting synthesis of astrin-1 to replenish its levels in G1.
source: CLUH may be implicated in supporting synthesis of astrin-1 to replenish its levels in G1.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section based on the observation that CLUH regulates astrin-1 synthesis.

claim: Depletion of astrin or kinastrin do not recapitulate the prominent mitochondrial defects observed upon CLUH downregulation or KO.
source: Our data do not support this scenario, since depletion of astrin or kinastrin do not recapitulate the prominent mitochondrial defects observed upon CLUH downregulation or KO.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: It is possible that the formation of the astrin-1–CLUH complex competes with the function of CLUH at the polysomes.
source: It is possible that the formation of the astrin-1–CLUH complex competes with the function of CLUH at the polysomes. This remains a hypothesis at present and more work will be required to assess this possibility.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: CLUH plays an essential role in the metabolic rewiring directed by mTORC1 signaling.
source: Our data establish an essential role of CLUH in the metabolic rewiring directed by mTORC1 signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on metabolomics data.

claim: Both CLUH KO and SPAG5 ind-KO cells showed inappropriate mTORC1 activation upon starvation.
source: Upon starvation, both CLUH KO and SPAG5 ind-KO cells showed inappropriate mTORC1 activation, in agreement with astrin being a negative regulator of mTORC1 (Thedieck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The metabolic defects caused by loss of CLUH were discordant with mTORC1 hyperactivation.
source: However, the metabolic defects caused by loss of CLUH were discordant with this signaling, with a decrease in the TCA cycle intermediates and in the pool of glycolytic intermediates, some nucleotides, and polyamines.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6.

claim: Enzymes of the TCA cycle as well as characteristic anaplerotic enzymes are encoded by bona fide CLUH target mRNAs.
source: Enzymes of the TCA cycle as well as characteristic anaplerotic enzymes, such as pyruvate carboxylase, proprionyl-CoA carboxylase, and other branched chain amino acid catabolic enzymes are encoded by bona fide CLUH target mRNAs (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Anaplerotic pathways are essential to replenish the TCA cycle intermediates to compensate for their loss upon activation of biosynthetic pathways following mTORC1 signaling.
source: These pathways are essential to replenish the TCA cycle intermediates to compensate for their loss upon activation of biosynthetic pathways following mTORC1 signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A compensatory increase in anaplerotic pathways occurs under conditions of chronic mTORC1 activation.
source: Indeed, a compensatory increase in anaplerotic pathways occurs under conditions of chronic mTORC1 activation (Dutchak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: CLUH tunes mTORC1 signaling in two independent ways: by regulating the expression of astrin-1 and by ensuring the maintenance of mitochondrial anaplerotic pathways via its RNA-binding function.
source: Therefore, CLUH tunes mTORC1 signaling in two independent ways, by regulating the expression of astrin-1 and by ensuring the maintenance of mitochondrial anaplerotic pathways via its RNA-binding function (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section based on all the data presented.

claim: mTORC1 positively regulates the translation of mitochondrial proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial dynamics.
source: mTORC1 positively regulates the translation of mitochondrial proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial dynamics (Morita et al., 2013; Morita et al., 2017), while inhibition of mTORC1 activates a lipid signaling cascade that triggers YME1L-mediated intramitochondrial proteolysis to limit mitochondrial biogenesis (MacVicar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 activates a lipid signaling cascade that triggers YME1L-mediated intramitochondrial proteolysis to limit mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: mTORC1 positively regulates the translation of mitochondrial proteins involved in oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial dynamics (Morita et al., 2013; Morita et al., 2017), while inhibition of mTORC1 activates a lipid signaling cascade that triggers YME1L-mediated intramitochondrial proteolysis to limit mitochondrial biogenesis (MacVicar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: mTORC1 hyperactivation is part of the integrated stress response that follows mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Furthermore, mTORC1 hyperactivation is part of the integrated stress response that follows mitochondrial dysfunction (Khan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Proliferating cells must shunt metabolites into mitochondrial pathways that promote cell growth or oxidative respiration and ATP production, depending on the cell cycle phase.
source: Proliferating cells must shunt metabolites into mitochondrial pathways that promote cell growth or oxidative respiration and ATP production, depending on the cell cycle phase (DeBerardinis et al., 2008; Salazar-Roa and Malumbres, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: In G1 cells double their mass and depend on glycolysis to fuel the TCA cycle and sustain biosynthetic pathways.
source: In G1 cells double their mass and depend on glycolysis to fuel the TCA cycle and sustain biosynthetic pathways, while in S synthesis of nucleotides is required and glutamine oxidation is prevalent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In S phase synthesis of nucleotides is required and glutamine oxidation is prevalent.
source: In G1 cells double their mass and depend on glycolysis to fuel the TCA cycle and sustain biosynthetic pathways, while in S synthesis of nucleotides is required and glutamine oxidation is prevalent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The TCA cycle intermediates fluctuate during the cell cycle.
source: Interestingly, the TCA cycle intermediates fluctuate during the cell cycle, and it is known that these variations are not transcriptionally regulated (Olsen et al., 2010; Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: The variations in TCA cycle intermediates during the cell cycle are not transcriptionally regulated.
source: Interestingly, the TCA cycle intermediates fluctuate during the cell cycle, and it is known that these variations are not transcriptionally regulated (Olsen et al., 2010; Ahn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: In mammalian cells, mTORC1 activation is important for the transition from G1 to S.
source: In mammalian cells, mTORC1 activation is important for the transition from G1 to S, an important check point when the energy levels and the growth status of the cell are sensed, and from G2 to M (Cuyàs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: In mammalian cells, mTORC1 activation is important for the transition from G2 to M.
source: In mammalian cells, mTORC1 activation is important for the transition from G1 to S, an important check point when the energy levels and the growth status of the cell are sensed, and from G2 to M (Cuyàs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: By regulating astrin-1 and stabilizing an RNA regulon involved in the TCA cycle and anaplerotic pathways, CLUH ensures that the progression of the cell cycle is adjusted with activation of mTORC1 signaling and the mitochondrial metabolic profile.
source: We hypothesize that by regulating astrin-1 and stabilizing an RNA regulon involved in the TCA cycle and anaplerotic pathways (Gao et al., 2014), CLUH ensures that the progression of the cell cycle is adjusted with activation of mTORC1 signaling and the mitochondrial metabolic profile (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion section based on all the data presented.

claim: Using a post-transcriptional mechanism to coordinate mitochondrial function with cell cycle phases allows a fast and flexible mean to control a broad gene program.
source: Using a post-transcriptional mechanism to coordinate mitochondrial function with cell cycle phases allows a fast and flexible mean to control a broad gene program.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Cells lacking CLUH have cell cycle defects, characterized by a faster cell cycle progression despite failure to properly double the cell mass.
source: Consistently, cells lacking CLUH have cell cycle defects, characterized by a faster cell cycle progression despite failure to properly double the cell mass.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Astrin is a component of centriolar satellites in interphase.
source: Astrin is a component of centriolar satellites in interphase, and it is required for the centrosomal localization of CDK5RAP2, a protein involved in microcephaly, and for proper centriole duplication in S phase (Thein et al., 2007; Kodani et al., 2015), a step which is crucial for cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: Astrin is required for the centrosomal localization of CDK5RAP2.
source: Astrin is a component of centriolar satellites in interphase, and it is required for the centrosomal localization of CDK5RAP2, a protein involved in microcephaly, and for proper centriole duplication in S phase (Thein et al., 2007; Kodani et al., 2015), a step which is crucial for cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: Astrin is required for proper centriole duplication in S phase.
source: Astrin is a component of centriolar satellites in interphase, and it is required for the centrosomal localization of CDK5RAP2, a protein involved in microcephaly, and for proper centriole duplication in S phase (Thein et al., 2007; Kodani et al., 2015), a step which is crucial for cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous work.

claim: Astrin-1 overexpression depletes endogenous CLUH from the cytoplasm and recruits it to structures that are close to centrosomes or contain centrosomal markers.
source: Astrin-1 overexpression depletes endogenous CLUH from the cytoplasm and recruits it to structures that are close to centrosomes or contain centrosomal markers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: Astrin was identified in an unbiased screen to be essential for the reentry in mitosis after DNA damage.
source: Finally, our data add to the evidence that astrin plays additional roles outside mitosis. Astrin was also identified in an unbiased screen to be essential for the reentry in mitosis after DNA damage (Halim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to previous work.

claim: HeLa cells overexpress not only astrin-1 but also astrin-2.
source: HeLa cells, as many human cancer cells, overexpress not only astrin-1 but also astrin-2, an isoform of astrin competent to bind all other interactors (kinastrin, DYLNN1, and MYCPB) and the kinetochore (Kern et al., 2017), but not CLUH.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by western blot data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Astrin-2 is competent to bind all other interactors (kinastrin, DYLNN1, and MYCPB) and the kinetochore, but not CLUH.
source: HeLa cells, as many human cancer cells, overexpress not only astrin-1 but also astrin-2, an isoform of astrin competent to bind all other interactors (kinastrin, DYLNN1, and MYCPB) and the kinetochore (Kern et al., 2017), but not CLUH.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of astrin-2 endows cancer cells with the ability to proliferate, despite a dysregulated coupling between mitochondrial metabolism and the cell cycle.
source: We propose that expression of astrin-2 endows cancer cells with the ability to proliferate, despite a dysregulated coupling between mitochondrial metabolism and the cell cycle, making CLUH a possible novel therapeutic target in cancers overexpressing SPAG5.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal in the Discussion section based on the findings.

claim: CLUH is a possible novel therapeutic target in cancers overexpressing SPAG5.
source: We propose that expression of astrin-2 endows cancer cells with the ability to proliferate, despite a dysregulated coupling between mitochondrial metabolism and the cell cycle, making CLUH a possible novel therapeutic target in cancers overexpressing SPAG5.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal in the Discussion section based on the findings.
